title: Topic Drill: Reading Informational Texts (Set C)

items.stem:
The Pell Hollow wind farm began feeding power to the county grid on Tuesday. Its twelve turbines stand along a ridge where steady winds blow most of the year. County officials said the farm can supply enough electricity for about four thousand homes. Engineers added special lights that glow only when a plane approaches, so the ridge stays dark at night for nearby residents.

Which sentence best states the main idea of the news brief?
options: A new wind farm now supplies power to the county grid.
Residents are unhappy about lights shining on the ridge.
Engineers are searching for a windier place to build turbines.
The county plans to close its older power plant this year.
items.explanation: The brief reports that the twelve-turbine farm started feeding the grid and can power about four thousand homes. The lights are a courtesy to neighbors, not a complaint. Nothing says engineers want another site, and the older plant is never mentioned, so those choices invent details.

items.stem:
Turbine blades at Pell Hollow turn slowly, about fifteen times each minute, yet their tips move quickly because the blades are long. A sensor on top of each tower measures wind speed. When gusts grow too strong, a motor tilts the blades so they catch less air, which protects the machine from damage. In calm weather the same motor tilts them back to catch more.

According to the passage, why does a motor tilt the blades during strong gusts?
options: To make the blades spin faster than fifteen times a minute
To measure how quickly the wind is moving overhead
To send extra electricity to the county grid at once
To catch less air and protect the turbine from damage
items.explanation: The passage says a motor tilts the blades so they catch less air, which protects the machine. Spinning faster would add strain, the sensor, not the motor, measures wind speed, and nothing links tilting to sending extra electricity to the grid. The detail about tilting is a direct cause and effect link, so rereading that sentence confirms the answer.

items.stem:
Marisol Quade, who manages the Pell Hollow site, checks each turbine by climbing its tower once a month. She carries a small tool bag and a tablet for notes. At the top she listens to the gearbox for odd rattles and wipes oil from the casing. Last spring she noticed a faint hum that did not match the others, and a crew replaced one bearing before the machine failed.

Which conclusion about Marisol is best supported by the passage?
options: She prefers working alone because crews slow her down.
Her careful listening helps prevent costly breakdowns.
She replaces every bearing in each tower herself.
She believes the turbines are too noisy for the ridge.
items.explanation: The hum she noticed led to a bearing swap before the machine failed, so her attentiveness prevents breakdowns. The passage never says she dislikes crews, a crew did the replacement, and she called a hum odd, not a reason the site is too noisy. Always check which actions the text credits to Marisol and which to the crew before inferring anything about her.

items.stem:
Letter to the editor: Last week’s article called the Pell Hollow turbines ugly, but I disagree. Each morning I walk my dog along the lower road, and the slow white blades remind me of a field of giant pinwheels. They are quiet, they pay for new school buses, and they give a once-empty ridge a purpose. Anyone who has stood beneath them could not call them a blemish.

What is the author’s main purpose in writing this letter?
options: To explain in great technical detail how turbines convert wind into electricity
To advertise walking routes near the lower road
To defend the turbines against a criticism printed earlier
To report a news story about the new school buses
items.explanation: The writer opens by answering last week’s article and then lists reasons the turbines are valuable, so the purpose is defense. The letter never explains the mechanics, the walking route is a passing detail, and school buses are a supporting point, not the news. The letter opens with a reference to last week’s article, which is the strongest clue to its purpose.

items.stem:
Our family is thrilled with the wind farm tour! The guide was patient, the hard hats fit the children, and standing inside a tower base felt like entering a giant, humming lighthouse. We learned more in one hour than a month of reading could teach. Honestly, the only sad moment was leaving. We are already planning to bring Grandpa next summer.

Which word best describes the tone of this review?
options: Skeptical
Enthusiastic
Indifferent
Resentful
items.explanation: The review uses words such as thrilled, giant humming lighthouse and sad to leave, and promises to return, all of which show enthusiasm. Skeptical would require doubt, indifferent would show no feeling, and resentful would show bitterness, none of which appear. Words like thrilled and already planning point to feeling, so tone answers should match that emotional vocabulary.

items.stem:
The weather office on Gannet Point finished upgrading its radar dish in March. The old dish scanned the sky every six minutes, which sometimes missed fast storms that formed and faded between sweeps. The new dish completes a scan in under two minutes. Forecasters now see rotation inside a cloud sooner and can send warnings to phones earlier. Staff call the change a quantum leap for the region’s safety.

As used in the passage, what does the phrase “quantum leap” most nearly mean?
options: A tiny adjustment made to old equipment
A leap in cost that surprised the staff
A sudden and very large improvement
A scientific theory about how clouds form
items.explanation: The passage contrasts six-minute scans with scans under two minutes and links the change to earlier warnings, so the phrase signals a big, sudden improvement. A tiny adjustment contradicts the contrast, cost is never discussed, and clouds are not explained by any theory in the text.

items.stem:
How a radar scan helps a forecaster: First, the dish sends out a pulse of radio waves. Next, the waves strike raindrops or hail and bounce back. Then a computer measures how long the echo took to return and how strong it was. Finally, it paints the result on a map, with brighter colors showing heavier rain.

How is the passage mainly organized?
options: As a comparison of two different machines
As a problem followed by several solutions
As a list of reasons with a final opinion
As a sequence of steps in a process
items.explanation: The words first, next, then and finally mark an ordered process from the pulse to the finished map. Only one machine is described, no problem is posed, and the text states no opinion, so comparison, problem and solution, and reasons do not fit. Words such as first, next and finally are signal words that reveal a sequence structure.

items.stem:
Because the new radar dish scans so quickly, the Gannet Point office now catches storms that last only ten minutes. Previously, forecasters sometimes learned of such storms only after reports arrived from drivers on the coast road. The faster scan also gives the staff time to double-check each warning, so fewer false alarms reach residents’ phones.

According to the passage, what is one effect of the faster scan?
options: Fewer false alarms are sent to residents.
Drivers on the coast road now report storms sooner.
Storms in the region now last only ten minutes.
Forecasters no longer need to double-check warnings.
items.explanation: The passage says the faster scan gives staff time to double-check, which means fewer false alarms. Drivers’ reports are what forecasters used to depend on, storm length is a natural fact the scan merely catches, and double-checking continues rather than ending. Notice that the stated effect comes from the word because, which links the faster scan to its result.

items.stem:
Text 1: The Gannet Point radar upgrade is worth every dollar. Faster scans mean earlier warnings, and earlier warnings save lives.

Text 2: The Gannet Point radar upgrade was a fine idea, but its price tag deserves a closer look. Money spent on the dish is money not spent on storm shelters, which also protect residents.

How do the two authors differ in their views of the upgrade?
options: Text 1 questions its cost, while Text 2 praises it fully.
Text 1 praises it fully, while Text 2 questions its cost.
Both texts agree that storm shelters matter more.
Neither text offers any opinion about the upgrade.
items.explanation: Text 1 states it is worth every dollar and points to safety, while Text 2 calls it a fine idea yet urges a closer look at the price. The reversal swaps the speakers, the shelters appear only in Text 2 as an alternative, and both texts clearly give opinions.

items.stem:
Forecaster Dev Santoro says the new radar made last month’s hailstorm easier to follow. “We saw the core of the storm tighten at 4:10,” the office log reads, “and warnings went out at 4:14.” Residents had four minutes to move their cars before the first stones fell at 4:18.

Which detail from the passage best supports the claim that the radar helped residents?
options: The office keeps a log of each storm it tracks.
The hailstorm happened during the previous month, according to the office log.
Warnings went out four minutes before the first stones fell.
Dev Santoro works as a forecaster at the office.
items.explanation: Evidence must show the radar helped residents act. The gap between a 4:14 warning and the 4:18 hail gave them time to move cars. A log, the month, and the job title are true but do not demonstrate any benefit to residents. Strong evidence is a specific fact that directly proves the claim rather than a general background detail.

items.stem:
For decades the Marrow Flats were drained so farmers could plant corn. This autumn, volunteers are reversing that work. Crews have removed old drainage pipes, and shallow pools are already filling with rain. Cattails, reeds and sedges will be planted in spring. Biologists expect herons, frogs and dragonflies to return within three years. They also expect the wetland to soak up floodwater that now rushes into the town below.

What is the main idea of the report?
options: Farmers are planning to grow more corn on the flats next spring.
Herons and frogs are leaving the area permanently.
Floods have grown worse since volunteers arrived.
A drained area is being restored to a natural wetland.
items.explanation: The report describes removing pipes, letting pools fill and planting reeds, which is restoration of a drained wetland. Corn farming is the past use, animals are expected to return, not leave, and floodwater is something the wetland should reduce, not worsen. Restoration here means returning the land to its natural state, which the pipes, pools and plantings all show.

items.stem:
A wetland acts like a sponge. When heavy rain falls, water spreads across the low ground and soaks into the soft soil instead of racing down a channel. Plants slow the flow even more, and their roots hold the soil in place. The water is released slowly in drier weeks, which is why a healthy wetland can keep a nearby stream running in summer.

Why does the author compare a wetland to a sponge?
options: To suggest that wetlands feel rough and dry to touch
To show how it absorbs water and releases it slowly
To explain why wetland plants have very long roots
To argue that a stream should never be disturbed
items.explanation: The comparison makes an abstract process familiar: a sponge soaks up water and lets it go gradually, just as the passage describes. Texture is not the point, roots are mentioned only for holding soil, and no argument about disturbing streams appears. Analogies work by mapping a familiar object onto an unfamiliar process, so match each part of the sponge to the wetland.

items.stem:
Volunteer notice: Planting day at the Marrow Flats is Saturday, April 12. Please meet at the gravel lot at eight. Bring waterproof boots, gloves and a water bottle, and wear clothes that can get muddy. Tools and seedlings will be provided. Children under twelve may come if an adult stays with them. The work ends at noon, and a light lunch will follow at the picnic shelter.

What should volunteers bring with them?
options: Waterproof boots, gloves and a water bottle
Shovels, seedlings and a picnic lunch
Only a signed form from an adult
Nothing, because everything is provided
items.explanation: The notice lists boots, gloves and a water bottle for volunteers. Tools and seedlings are supplied, lunch is provided, and an adult only needs to stay with children under twelve. Saying nothing is needed ignores the items the notice asks them to bring. Reread the sentence that lists what volunteers should bring and separate it from what the organizers supply.

items.stem:
Ranger Helena Orsk first walked the Marrow Flats as a child, when the land was dry enough for tractors. Now, wearing tall boots, she wades through ankle-deep water to count nesting sites. “I used to cross here on a dusty track,” she tells the volunteers, and her voice drops. “Seeing a heron stand where my boots once raised dust is something I never thought I would live to see.”

Which statement about Helena can be inferred from the passage?
options: She believes the project will fail within three years.
She learned to drive a tractor on the flats.
She is unhappy that volunteers are walking through the water.
She is moved by the change she has watched over her lifetime.
items.explanation: Her lowered voice and the contrast between dust and a heron show deep feeling about the transformation. Nothing suggests she expects failure, the tractors in the passage are only a detail about dry land, and she is welcoming the volunteers, not resenting them. Helena’s tone and word choice, not any direct statement of feeling, are the clues that support this inference.

items.stem:
Before restoration, rain on the Marrow Flats ran off quickly through underground pipes. As a result, the creek in town rose fast after each storm and sometimes spilled over the main street. Now that the pipes are gone, the water lingers on the flats for days. Officials say the town’s streets have stayed dry through the last three storms.

What is the cause of the creek rising quickly in the past?
options: Cattails and reeds grew too thickly along the banks.
Volunteers removed the pipes during the autumn.
Rain ran off rapidly through underground pipes.
Officials stopped checking the town’s streets.
items.explanation: The passage states that rain left the flats quickly through pipes, so the creek rose fast. The plants are part of the restoration, removing pipes is what fixed the problem, and officials checking streets is unrelated to the creek’s rise. A cause explains why something happened, and here the passage names it in the sentence about pipes and quick runoff.

items.stem:
Riders in the Larkspur district can now track buses on their phones. The new RideNow app shows each bus as a moving dot on a map and predicts its arrival at your stop. The transit office built the app after a survey found that most riders waited longer than they wished for buses they could not see. The app is free and works on most phones made in the past six years.

What was the main reason the transit office built the app?
options: Riders disliked waiting for buses they could not see.
Newer phones can no longer read paper schedules.
Buses in the district had begun running more slowly.
Survey results showed riders wanted to pay less for fares.
items.explanation: The brief says a survey revealed riders waited longer than they wished for buses they could not see, which led to the app. Phones and paper schedules are not linked, bus speed is never described, and fares were not part of the survey as reported.

items.stem:
The RideNow app is not perfect. Because it relies on signals from buses, a dot can freeze in tunnels or beneath tall buildings. During a snowstorm last week, one rider reported that a dot stayed in place for eleven minutes while the bus kept moving. Still, the transit office says such freezes affect only a small share of trips and that an update will reduce them.

What can be concluded about the transit office’s attitude toward the app?
options: It believes the app has no real problems.
It admits flaws but expects to improve the app.
It plans to remove the app after the winter season is over.
It blames riders for the frozen dots.
items.explanation: The office acknowledges freezing, calls it a small share of trips and promises an update, which shows realistic confidence. Denying problems contradicts the admission, removal is never mentioned, and the dots freeze because of signals, not rider behavior. Main idea questions ask for the reason behind the whole passage, not a minor detail about phones or cities.

items.stem:
Text 1: The RideNow app is the best change our buses have seen in years. I stopped sprinting for the bus because the map tells me when to leave my door.

Text 2: I appreciate the map on RideNow, but I rely on printed timetables when my phone battery is low. A bus stop sign with a posted schedule never needs charging.

What do both writers acknowledge?
options: Printed timetables are outdated and should be removed from every bus stop.
Phones should be charged during every bus trip.
Knowing when the bus will arrive is valuable to riders.
Running to catch a bus is good exercise.
items.explanation: Both texts value timely information: Text 1 leaves home on the map’s advice, and Text 2 praises both the map and posted schedules. Neither calls timetables outdated, advises charging during trips, or praises running as exercise. An inference must rest on what the office actually says, and here it says both that freezes occur and that fixes are coming.

items.stem:
Using the app takes only a few steps. Open RideNow, then allow it to use your location so it can find the nearest stop. Tap the stop to see a list of routes. Choose your route, and the app displays a countdown in minutes. You can also tap the bell icon to receive an alert when your bus is two stops away.

Which sentence best describes the author’s purpose?
options: To persuade readers to ride the bus more often
To entertain readers with a story about commuting
To compare the app with a competing product
To instruct readers on how to use the app
items.explanation: The passage walks the reader through ordered actions such as opening the app, tapping a stop and choosing a route, which is instructional. It never urges more riding, tells a story, or mentions another product. Look for what both writers share rather than what separates them, since the question asks about common ground.

items.stem:
The app’s creator, Ines Valdor, spent nine months testing it with riders who had never used a transit map before. She watched them hesitate over small buttons and misread the colors, then redesigned the screens. “If a first-time rider cannot use it in half a minute,” she says, “then I have not finished.”

As used in the passage, what does the word “hesitate” most nearly mean?
options: Pause because of uncertainty
Hurry through without thinking
Argue loudly with the designer
Refuse to touch the screen at all
items.explanation: Riders unfamiliar with the screens would pause while deciding what to press, which matches pausing from uncertainty. Hurrying is the opposite, arguing is not described, and refusing to touch the screen is too extreme since they used small buttons and misread colors. Purpose is revealed by what the text does, and instructions with ordered actions signal that the author wants to teach.

items.stem:
Rural broadband update: The Tamsin Valley Co-op has finished laying fiber cable along Route 9, and about two hundred farms and homes can now sign up for high-speed internet. Crews buried the cable beside the road instead of stringing it on poles, which protects it from ice storms. Sign-ups open on the first of the month at the co-op office or by phone.

Which detail explains why the cable was buried?
options: Poles along Route 9 were too expensive to buy.
Farms asked crews to keep wires out of sight.
Burying it protects the cable from ice storms.
Sign-ups open on the first of the month.
items.explanation: The brief gives one reason for burial: it protects the cable from ice storms. Cost of poles and the farms’ wishes are never stated, and the sign-up date is a separate detail about how residents enroll, not why crews chose burial. Evidence for a reason is the sentence that gives the reason itself, not a detail about timing or cost.

items.stem:
Before the fiber arrived, Tamsin Valley students often drove to the library parking lot to use its wireless signal for homework. Some sat in cars until nine at night. Teachers had to plan assignments that could be finished offline, and farmers could not check grain prices without a long drive. Residents say the new cable removes a daily burden they had stopped noticing.

What does the passage suggest about life before the fiber?
options: Students preferred doing homework in parked cars.
Teachers refused to give any homework assignments.
Farmers had no interest in grain prices.
Poor internet access forced residents to arrange their routines around it.
items.explanation: Students driving to a lot, teachers planning offline work and farmers making long drives show routines bent around poor access. Preference for cars is not stated, teachers still assigned work, and farmers wanted prices but could not get them easily. The inference rests on several linked examples, which together reveal how daily routines were arranged around the weak signal.

items.stem:
Dear neighbors: I was skeptical when the co-op first proposed the fiber project, since it asked each household to pay a one-time fee. Now that my video calls with my daughter’s family run smoothly, I regret my doubt. I encourage anyone still hesitating to attend the meeting on Thursday, where co-op staff will explain the payment plan.

Which statement best describes the author’s attitude change?
options: She moved from enthusiasm to anger.
She moved from doubt to approval.
She has been indifferent from the start.
She still opposes the project but attends meetings.
items.explanation: She begins skeptical, then regrets her doubt after video calls improve, and urges others to attend, a shift from doubt to approval. Anger never appears, indifference contradicts her strong feelings, and she no longer opposes the project. Track the author’s words from the first sentence to the last to see the direction in which her opinion moved.

items.stem:
The co-op compares two options. Plan Basic costs thirty dollars a month and offers speeds suitable for email, shopping and video calls. Plan Plus costs fifty dollars a month and supports several people streaming at once, as well as large file uploads. A household that mostly sends email and reads news will likely find Basic sufficient.

How is the passage mainly organized?
options: By comparing two choices and recommending one use for each
By telling a story about a family’s internet problems during a long winter
By listing causes of slow internet in rural areas
By describing the steps for burying a cable
items.explanation: The text sets two plans side by side, with cost and capabilities, and indicates who would suit Basic. It tells no family story, does not examine causes of slowness, and says nothing about installation steps. Structure questions ask how the information is arranged, and here the two plans are presented in parallel for comparison.

items.stem:
A co-op report states that call quality improved after the fiber connection. Before the upgrade, video calls from the valley froze an average of six times in a ten-minute call. After the upgrade, a test of twenty calls showed only one freeze in the whole group.

Which evidence best supports the claim that call quality improved?
options: Twenty calls were tested by the co-op.
The number of freezes fell from six per call to one in twenty calls.
The upgrade involved installing fiber cable.
A video call usually lasts about ten minutes.
items.explanation: The claim is supported by the before and after comparison of freezes. The number of test calls, the nature of the upgrade and the typical call length describe the setup but do not show any improvement in quality. The best evidence offers numbers that can be compared directly, which proves a change rather than just describing a test.

items.stem:
The Eastgate Community Kitchen serves a hot meal every weekday at noon, and nobody is asked to prove need or pay a fee. Volunteers chop vegetables from a nearby garden, simmer large pots of soup and set tables for about ninety guests. The kitchen opened six years ago in a former bakery and now depends on twenty regular volunteers.

Which title best fits this profile?
options: A Free Daily Meal Built by Volunteers
How a Bakery Became a Famous Restaurant
The Cost of Feeding Ninety People
Gardening Tips for Busy Families
items.explanation: The profile centers on free weekday meals prepared by regular volunteers. The bakery is only the building’s history, costs are never discussed, and the garden is a source of vegetables rather than the topic, so those titles miss the main idea. A good title covers the whole profile, so check that it names the free meal and the volunteers who prepare it.

items.stem:
Head cook Bram Okoye describes his job as part planning, part puzzle. Deliveries arrive without warning, so he rarely knows on Monday what he will cook on Friday. One week a farm sent forty pounds of squash, and the kitchen served squash soup, squash bread and roasted squash for four days. “You learn to say yes first and work out the menu later,” he laughs.

What does the passage suggest about Bram?
options: He dislikes squash and avoids serving it.
He plans each weekly menu a month in advance.
He adapts cheerfully to whatever ingredients arrive.
He refuses donations that arrive unexpectedly.
items.explanation: Bram says yes first and plans later, laughs about it and makes four days of squash dishes, which shows cheerful flexibility. He serves squash, cannot plan far ahead because deliveries are unpredictable, and accepts donations rather than refusing them. Bram’s own quoted words reveal his attitude more reliably than any detail about the squash itself.

items.stem:
Volunteer shifts at the Eastgate Community Kitchen run in two parts. The prep shift, from nine to eleven, is for chopping, washing and measuring. The service shift, from eleven to one, is for serving guests and washing dishes. Volunteers under sixteen may join only the service shift, and everyone must wash hands before touching food.

Who may join the prep shift?
options: Volunteers who are younger than sixteen
Only guests who stay for the noon meal
Only the head cook and his helpers
Volunteers who are sixteen or older
items.explanation: The notice limits volunteers under sixteen to the service shift, so the prep shift is open to those sixteen or older. Guests are not mentioned as prep workers, and nothing restricts prep to the head cook. Restrictions are stated as exceptions, so work out who is left over once the under-sixteen limit is applied.

items.stem:
When the Eastgate Community Kitchen began offering a weekend takeout bag, attendance at the weekday meal actually rose. Organizers had feared the opposite. They now believe that families who first accepted a bag felt comfortable enough to try a sit-down lunch. The weekend program also gave volunteers who work on weekdays a chance to help.

What is the best summary of this passage?
options: Weekday meals were canceled entirely because the takeout program grew too popular.
A weekend takeout program unexpectedly brought more people to weekday meals.
Volunteers prefer weekends to weekdays for all jobs.
Organizers were certain the takeout bag would succeed.
items.explanation: The passage reports that weekday attendance rose after takeout began, contrary to fears. No meals were canceled, volunteer preference is a minor detail, and the organizers feared the opposite, so they were not certain of success. A summary must include the surprising result, so the best choice reports both the program and its unexpected effect.

items.stem:
The kitchen’s newsletter thanks Pearl Dunmore, who donated a commercial dishwasher after hearing that volunteers spent three hours scrubbing plates by hand each day. “I wanted to give something that gives time back,” she wrote. The newsletter adds that the machine will let volunteers spend more time talking with guests.

Which word best describes the tone of the newsletter toward Pearl?
options: Grateful
Doubtful
Mocking
Detached
items.explanation: The newsletter thanks Pearl and explains how her gift helps volunteers, a grateful tone. Doubtful would suggest uncertainty about the gift, mocking would ridicule her, and detached would show no emotion, none of which fits the warm acknowledgment. Tone is shown by word choice, and the newsletter’s thanks and explanation of the gift all point to gratitude.

items.stem:
The Cobalt Hill Observatory opens its doors to the public on the second Friday of every month. Visitors can look through a thirty-inch telescope, hear a short talk about the evening sky and walk the dark path to the dome. Because light spoils the view, flashlights must have red covers, which the gift shop sells for one dollar.

Why must visitors use flashlights with red covers?
options: Red covers make the path easier to find.
The gift shop needs money to repair the dome.
Red light is required by the thirty-inch telescope.
White light would spoil the dark view of the sky.
items.explanation: The notice says light spoils the view, which is why the covers are needed. The gift shop merely sells them, the path is already described as dark, not hard to find, and the telescope is not said to require red light. The question asks for a reason, and the passage supplies it in the sentence explaining what light does to the view of the sky.

items.stem:
A telescope works much like a bucket collecting rain. The bigger the opening, the more light it gathers. A wide mirror collects far more than the human eye, so faint objects that look invisible become clear. This is why the Cobalt Hill dome uses a thirty-inch mirror instead of a smaller one.

What is the effect of using a wider mirror?
options: The telescope becomes much easier to carry to the dome by hand.
The sky appears darker for the visitors nearby.
More light is collected, making faint objects visible.
Rain collects in the bucket more slowly.
items.explanation: The passage compares a mirror to a bucket and says a wider opening gathers more light, so faint objects become clear. Portability, a darker sky and slower rain are not claimed, and the bucket is only an analogy. Cause and effect appears in the word wider and its result, more light, which the bucket comparison makes easy to picture.

items.stem:
Text 1: Stargazing is best done far from town. At Cobalt Hill, the glow of streetlamps is faint, so even a beginner can see hundreds of stars.

Text 2: I live in the middle of town, yet from my rooftop I can still see the moon, several planets and a few bright stars. Not every sky watcher needs a remote hill.

Which statement describes a difference between the two texts?
options: Text 1 describes rooftops across the whole town, while Text 2 describes streetlamps on the hill road.
Text 1 discusses planets, while Text 2 discusses telescopes.
Both texts say stargazing is impossible in town.
Text 1 stresses dark locations, while Text 2 shows that some viewing is possible in town.
items.explanation: Text 1 recommends a dark, distant site, while Text 2 argues that sky watching can occur in town. The options mixing rooftops and streetlamps, planets and telescopes, or claiming impossibility in town misreport what each text says. Compare the central point of each text separately, then test every option against both before choosing.

items.stem:
Lena Park started volunteering at the observatory at fourteen, mostly to carry equipment. Over time, the staff taught her to align the telescope, and last autumn she led a tour for twenty visitors. Standing beneath the open dome, she described a distant cluster of stars so vividly that a child asked if she had traveled there.

Which inference is best supported by the passage?
options: Lena’s skills and confidence grew during her time at the observatory.
Lena has visited the cluster of stars in person.
The staff would rather not spend their evenings training young volunteers at the dome.
Visitors found the tour boring and left early.
items.explanation: She moved from carrying equipment to aligning the telescope and leading a tour, so her skills grew. The child’s question shows how vivid her description was, not actual travel. The staff trained her willingly, and no visitor leaving early is mentioned. An inference should be supported by the sequence of her tasks, from carrying equipment to leading twenty visitors, not by the child’s question.

items.stem:
The observatory’s website invites everyone to share a night with the stars. It promises friendly guides, warm cocoa and a view you will never forget. Its closing line urges families to reserve seats early, because Friday sessions fill within days.

What is the author’s main purpose in writing the website text?
options: To explain how the telescope mirror is made
To encourage people to attend and reserve a place
To warn visitors about the cost of cocoa
To report on a scientific discovery
items.explanation: The text uses inviting language and ends by urging early reservations, aiming to attract attendees. It never discusses mirror manufacturing, cocoa costs or discoveries. Persuasive language such as invites, promises and urges signals a purpose of encouraging attendance, not informing or warning, which is why the invitation matters here.

items.stem:
The Kettleby Tool Library has found a second life for unwanted hand tools. Residents drop off rusty hammers, cracked saws and loose screwdrivers at the recycling shed, where retired carpenters clean, sharpen and repair them. Once restored, the tools are lent out to neighbors free of charge. In its first year the program saved nearly nine hundred tools from the landfill and lent them to about three hundred households.

What is the main idea of this news brief?
options: Retired carpenters are leaving the town of Kettleby.
Landfills in the region are running out of space.
A local program repairs old tools and lends them out.
Households must pay a fee to borrow any tool.
items.explanation: The brief explains that donated tools are repaired by carpenters and lent for free, which is the central point. Carpenters are not leaving, landfill capacity is not discussed, and borrowing is free of charge. A main idea covers the whole brief, including repair, lending and the free service, rather than a single number or detail.

items.stem:
To restore a rusty hand saw, volunteers follow four stages. First, they soak the blade in vinegar to loosen the rust. Second, they scrub it with a wire brush until the metal shines. Third, they file each tooth to a sharp edge. Last, they rub oil on the blade to keep moisture away.

Why do volunteers rub oil on the blade as the last step?
options: To loosen the rust before scrubbing begins
To sharpen each tooth along the blade
To make the blade easier to soak in vinegar
To keep moisture from causing new rust
items.explanation: The passage states that the oil keeps moisture away, which prevents rust from returning. Loosening rust is the vinegar’s job, filing sharpens teeth, and soaking happens first, not after the oil. Ordered words such as first, second and last make it easy to find the reason for each stage in the process.

items.stem:
Shed manager Odalys Revere insists that every tool leaves in better shape than it arrived. A recent donation of garden shears had been locked tight for years. She spent an afternoon with penetrating oil and patience until the blades moved smoothly. “Nobody should borrow a tool that fights back,” she told the volunteers, and then hung the shears on the wall.

What does the passage suggest about Odalys?
options: She takes pride in quality and wants borrowers to have good tools.
She prefers to throw away tools that are hard to fix.
She is annoyed by volunteers who ask questions.
She sells the repaired tools to raise money.
items.explanation: She spends an afternoon freeing locked shears and declares nobody should borrow a tool that fights back, showing pride in quality. She does not discard tools, nothing about annoyance appears, and the tools are lent free, not sold. Her actions, the afternoon of patient work, and her quoted words together reveal her values more strongly than any single statement.

items.stem:
Memo to staff: Beginning next month, the tool library will close on Mondays so volunteers can complete repairs without interruptions. The shed will remain open Tuesday through Saturday, from ten until four. Anyone who has borrowed a tool due on a Monday may return it on Tuesday without a late fee.

What is the main purpose of the memo?
options: To ask volunteers to join a repair workshop
To explain how to sharpen a saw
To announce a change in the library’s schedule
To thank borrowers for returning tools early
items.explanation: The memo tells staff about a new Monday closure and the open days, which announces a schedule change. It does not request workshop volunteers, give sharpening directions, or thank anyone for early returns. Purpose is found by asking what the reader is meant to do or know after reading, and here it is the new schedule.

items.stem:
Text 1: Buying a new hammer is quick, but a repaired one from the tool library works just as well and costs nothing.

Text 2: A borrowed tool is only useful if it fits the job. For large projects, owning your own tools may save repeated trips to the shed.

Which statement best compares the two texts?
options: Text 1 favors owning every tool you use, while Text 2 favors borrowing from the shed in all cases.
Text 1 favors borrowing for savings, while Text 2 notes that owning can suit big projects.
Both texts say repaired tools are unsafe.
Both texts describe how volunteers repair hammers.
items.explanation: Text 1 stresses that a repaired tool costs nothing, while Text 2 points out that owning may be more convenient for large projects. The reversed preferences, safety claims and repair descriptions do not appear in either text. Comparison items require checking what each text emphasizes, so compare their central points before reading the choices.

items.stem:
On Saturday, more than a hundred volunteers waded and paddled along a three-mile stretch of the Willow Bend River, collecting trash from the banks and shallows. By evening, they had filled sixty bags with bottles, cans and plastic wrap, and hauled out two bicycle frames and a rusted shopping cart. Organizers say the river looks cleaner than it has in years and plan another effort in the fall.

Which sentence best states the main idea of the report?
options: Bicycle frames are the most common litter found in rivers, according to the organizers.
The river cleanup was canceled because of bad weather.
Organizers believe the river can never be fully cleaned.
Volunteers removed a large amount of trash from the Willow Bend River.
items.explanation: The report describes a hundred volunteers filling sixty bags and hauling out larger items, so the central point is the amount of trash removed. Bicycle frames were only two items, the event happened, and organizers plan a fall effort, which is hopeful, not defeated. A main idea summarizes the entire event, which makes the amount of trash removed more central than any single object.

items.stem:
Litter harms a river in several ways. Plastic breaks into tiny pieces that fish mistake for food. Cans and bottles collect in slow pools, where they trap insects and block sunlight needed by water plants. Over time, the loss of plants leaves less oxygen in the water, and fewer fish can survive.

According to the passage, what is the final result of the loss of water plants?
options: More plastic that fish mistake for food
Less oxygen in the water, so fewer fish can live there
Faster flow through the river’s slow pools during the summer months
More sunlight reaching the insects below
items.explanation: The text traces a chain: litter blocks sunlight, plants decline, oxygen drops and fewer fish survive. Plastic pieces are an earlier harm, nothing says flow speeds up, and the sunlight is blocked, not increased. Follow the chain in the order given, from litter to sunlight to plants to oxygen, and choose the last link.

items.stem:
Dear volunteers: Thank you for giving your Saturday to the river. I walked the bank on Monday and saw herons wading where we had hauled out bags of cans. Your work is already making a difference. Please keep an eye out for the next event, and bring a friend who has not yet joined us.

How does the author feel about the volunteers’ work?
options: Appreciative and hopeful
Critical and impatient
Confused and uncertain
Bored and distant
items.explanation: The thank you, the observation of herons and the encouragement to bring a friend show appreciation and hope. Critical, confused or bored attitudes do not match the warm and specific praise in the letter. Tone is carried by phrases such as thank you and already making a difference, which show warmth rather than criticism.

items.stem:
The cleanup crew wore waders and carried grabbers, but the real challenge was the mud. Several volunteers lost a boot in the thick silt and had to be pulled free by teammates. By noon, laughter echoed across the water as the group invented a game: whoever lifted the strangest object would win an extra cookie at lunch.

Which meaning of the word “silt” fits the passage?
options: A rough rope tied to the bank
A type of trash made from plastic
Fine mud carried by water and settled on the bottom
A shallow flat boat used to cross the river in summer, when water is low
items.explanation: The passage says volunteers lost boots in thick silt, which points to soft, fine mud on the riverbed. Rope, plastic trash and a boat would not trap a boot in this way. Context clues, such as boots stuck while wading, narrow the meaning of an unfamiliar word to fine, soft mud.

items.stem:
The cleanup organizers posted a notice saying that the river is healthier now. The notice states that volunteers counted twenty-two fish species in a quick survey, and that the same survey last year found only fifteen.

Which evidence from the passage best supports the claim that the river is healthier?
options: The organizers posted a notice about the river on a public bulletin board.
The survey found twenty-two fish species, up from fifteen last year.
The survey was done quickly by volunteers.
Volunteers worked on the river for a day.
items.explanation: Evidence must show improvement, and the rise from fifteen to twenty-two species does so. The notice itself, the speed of the survey and the day of work do not prove the river’s condition changed. A claim of improvement needs numbers that show change over time, which only the comparison of surveys provides.

items.stem:
The Brightwater Middle School robotics team travelled to the regional competition with a robot named Gizmo. Teams must program a robot to move small cubes into marked zones in two minutes. Gizmo scored well in the first round but stalled in the second when a loose wire cut its power. The students repaired it between rounds and finished fourth among twenty teams.

What is the main idea of the news brief?
options: Gizmo won the competition in both rounds.
Wires should never be used to power robots in any school competition.
A student team overcame a mechanical problem and placed well.
The competition was limited to four teams.
items.explanation: The brief reports that Gizmo lost power from a loose wire, was repaired between rounds and finished fourth of twenty. It did not win both rounds, the wire was a single failure, and twenty teams took part. The brief spends most of its words on the setback and the repair, so the idea of overcoming a problem is central.

items.stem:
Coach Priya Anand tells new members that failure is part of the design process. She keeps a shelf of broken parts in the lab, each labeled with a lesson. A bent axle reminds them to test weight limits, and a fried circuit board reminds them to check wiring twice. “A robot that never breaks,” she likes to say, “has never been pushed.”

What is the author’s main purpose in describing the shelf?
options: To show how mistakes can be treated as useful lessons
To argue that robots should be made from cheaper parts
To explain why the school lacks lab space
To advertise replacement axles for sale
items.explanation: The shelf of labeled broken parts demonstrates that Coach Anand turns failures into learning. Cost of parts, lab space and sales are not topics of the passage. Purpose questions ask why the author included a detail, and here the labeled shelf demonstrates a belief about learning from mistakes.

items.stem:
Competition schedule: Check-in opens at 8:00 a.m., and teams must have their robots inspected by 9:00. Qualifying rounds run from 9:30 until 12:00. A lunch break follows, with finals beginning at 1:15 p.m. Awards will be presented at 3:00 in the main hall. Robots that fail inspection may be repaired once and brought back before 9:30.

According to the schedule, when do the finals begin?
options: At 9:30 a.m., after inspection
At 12:00, when qualifying rounds end
At 3:00 p.m., with the awards
At 1:15 p.m., after the lunch break
items.explanation: The schedule states that finals begin at 1:15 p.m. after lunch. Qualifying rounds start at 9:30, they end at 12:00 followed by lunch, and awards are presented at 3:00. Schedule questions require matching a time to an event, so read the line about finals and ignore the nearby times.

items.stem:
Text 1: Robotics teams teach students to build, code and work together. These skills carry over to nearly any career.

Text 2: Robotics competitions can be expensive. Kits, travel and fees add up, and families with less money may feel left out.

What is a main difference between the two texts?
options: Text 1 raises a concern about expense, while Text 2 highlights benefits of building skills.
Text 1 discusses fees, while Text 2 discusses careers.
Text 1 highlights benefits, while Text 2 raises a concern about cost.
Both texts argue that robotics should be discontinued.
items.explanation: Text 1 praises skills gained, while Text 2 points to expenses that can exclude families. Swapping the roles, the topics or claiming both want robotics ended misstates the texts. Text 1 and Text 2 each focus on a different side of robotics, so the key identifies both emphases correctly.

items.stem:
Because Gizmo’s gripper was too wide, the robot dropped cubes during the first practice run. The students measured the cubes and narrowed the gripper by half an inch. In the next run, Gizmo carried every cube without a slip.

What caused Gizmo to drop the cubes at first?
options: The cubes were heavier than the robot allowed.
The students did not measure the cubes at all.
The practice run lasted too long.
The gripper was too wide for the cubes.
items.explanation: The passage states the gripper was too wide, so cubes slipped. Weight is never mentioned, the students measured the cubes only after the problem, and run length is not discussed. Cause and effect appears here with the word because, followed by the repair that fixed the problem in the next run.

items.stem:
The Ferrow Junction Rail Museum fills a restored depot with the history of local railways. Its centerpiece is a steam engine from the early twentieth century that hauled coal and passengers across the valley. Visitors may climb into the cab, ring the bell and read old tickets in glass cases. A model railroad in the back room shows how the junction looked when five lines met there.

What is the main idea of the passage?
options: The museum preserves local railway history through hands-on displays.
The steam engine still carries passengers across the valley each day of the week.
Five rail lines still meet at the junction.
The depot was built to store coal for the valley.
items.explanation: The passage describes a depot museum offering an engine to climb, bells to ring, tickets and a model. It does not say the engine runs, the five lines refer to the past, and coal was only cargo hauled. The best main idea names the museum’s purpose and its method, rather than a fact about the engine or the junction.

items.stem:
The museum’s guide, Tobias Lind, says the steam engine was an ordinary workhorse, not a star. For forty years it pulled slow coal trains and rarely drew a crowd. After it was retired, townspeople gathered to say goodbye as if it were a hometown hero. “People loved it,” Tobias says, “because it was part of everyday life.”

Which inference is best supported by the passage?
options: Coal trains were famous across the whole country.
Familiarity can make an ordinary object meaningful to a community.
The townspeople were glad to see the old steam engine finally retired from service.
Tobias believes the engine was never useful.
items.explanation: The engine was ordinary yet loved because it was part of everyday life, so familiarity gave it meaning. Fame across the country is not claimed, the farewell shows sadness, and Tobias calls it a workhorse, not useless. An inference goes one step beyond the text, and here the farewell gathering is the clue about the community’s feelings.

items.stem:
The Municipal Library has begun digitizing its collection of old newspapers. Each page is placed on a flat scanner, photographed and then processed by software that turns the printed words into text. Staff then proofread the text to correct mistakes. Once finished, readers will be able to search for any name or event from home instead of paging through fragile paper.

How is the passage organized?
options: As a debate between supporters and critics
As a list of old newspapers in the library
As a comparison of scanners and cameras
As a sequence of steps followed by the benefit to readers
items.explanation: The passage walks through scanning, processing and proofreading, and ends with what readers gain. No debate, list of papers or scanner comparison appears. Words such as placed, photographed, processed and proofread signal a sequence of steps, and the final sentence states the benefit that readers will gain from home.

items.stem:
Digitizing is slow work. Newsprint grows brittle with age, and some pages crumble at the edges. Conservator Amara Fenn handles each sheet with cotton gloves and a soft brush, and she sometimes spends an hour on a single page. She says the time is worthwhile, because a fragile page scanned once can be studied by thousands without being touched again.

As used in the passage, what does the word “fragile” most nearly mean?
options: Unusually expensive
Easily damaged
Brightly colored
Difficult to read
items.explanation: The passage says pages crumble and must be handled gently, which shows they are easily damaged. Cost, color and readability are not what the details describe. Vocabulary in context depends on nearby details, and the gloves, soft brush and crumbling edges all point to damage.

items.stem:
Text 1: Putting newspapers online helps students research local history from home, saving trips to the library.

Text 2: Some older residents prefer holding the actual paper. They say screens cannot replace the smell and feel of old pages, even if searching is faster.

Which statement best describes the relationship between the two texts?
options: Text 1 stresses convenience, while Text 2 notes a preference for the original.
Both texts argue that digitizing should stop.
Text 2 describes in detail how the scanning process works step by step in the library.
Text 1 says residents prefer paper newspapers.
items.explanation: Text 1 values research convenience, while Text 2 values the physical experience even while admitting speed. Neither wants digitizing stopped, Text 2 does not explain scanning, and the paper preference belongs to Text 2. Both texts describe digitizing from a different human viewpoint, so the correct choice captures convenience on one side and preference for paper on the other.
